candidate.answerReason: The other two sides can be written as \(u\le27-u\), with \(4\le u\le13\). Heron's formula gives an integer area only for \(u=10\), producing sides 10, 17, 21 and area 84.

methods.label: Use Heron's formula and check the finite possibilities
methods.explanation:
The two sides other than 21 sum to \(48-21=27\). Call them \(u\) and \(27-u\), choosing \(u\le27-u\) so that each unordered pair is considered once. Then \(u\le13\), because \(u\) is an integer. The triangle inequality
\[
u+21>27-u
\]
gives \(u>3\). Thus exactly the integers \(4\le u\le13\) need consideration. The other triangle inequalities hold throughout this range, and \(u\) is the shortest side because \(u\le13<21\).

The semiperimeter is \(s=48/2=24\). Heron's formula for the positive area \(K\) gives
\[
K^2=24(24-21)(24-u)(u-3)
=36N,
\qquad N=2(u-3)(24-u).
\]
If \(K\) is an integer, \(36\mid K^2\) forces \(6\mid K\), since squaring doubles every prime exponent. Consequently \(N=(K/6)^2\) must be a perfect square. Conversely, a perfect-square \(N\) gives the integer area \(6\sqrt N\).

For \(u=4,5,6,7,8\), the values of \(N\) are
\[
40,\ 76,\ 108,\ 136,\ 160.
\]
For \(u=9,10,11,12,13\), they are
\[
180,\ 196,\ 208,\ 216,\ 220.
\]
Checking the integer squares from \(6^2=36\) through \(15^2=225\), the only square in these lists is \(196=14^2\), occurring at \(u=10\).

The resulting sides are \(10,17,21\), and their area is \(6\cdot14=84\), an integer. All possible side pairs have been checked, so the shortest side is \(\boxed{10}\), choice \(\boxed{\text{B}}\).
